synopsis: Hydra-0 represents actions as visible point trajectories and transports initial-image latent features along them to condition future-video generation. Robot commands supply these trajectories in forward mode; desired object motion supplies them in inverse mode, where supervised heads read executable actions from denoised transformer features. The strongest evidence concerns predicted motion and recorded-trajectory replay. Physical control is demonstrated qualitatively on one flexible-pipe-bending task. [E03, E05, E08, E11, E15, E16]

problem.text: Native joint and end-effector commands require video models to learn embodiment-dependent mappings from commands to visible motion. The authors seek a shared visual interface that can learn interaction consequences from heterogeneous robot and human videos while retaining a route to executable robot commands.

contributions.text: A visibility-aware trajectory interface connects video-derived training conditions with deployment conditions obtained from controller-and-physics rollouts, robot geometry and camera calibration.

Action flow is implemented across Cosmos 2.5 and two Wan2.2 variants. The same-backbone Cosmos comparison provides more direct evidence about the conditioning representation than the strongest cross-backbone comparison.

The authors extend the interface to open-loop policy evaluation and inverse control without task-specific expert robot demonstrations. The inverse mode nevertheless requires paired robot trajectories and executed-action supervision.

inputs: Initial RGB observation and pretrained text/image conditioning context. [E05, E06]
Forward deployment: candidate robot commands, robot geometry, controller-and-physics rollout, and camera calibration. [E03]
Inverse deployment: desired object flow extracted from a held-out human demonstration, with embodiment flow excluded. [E08, E16]
outputs: Forward mode: predicted future visual latents and optionally decoded RGB observations. [E05]
Inverse mode: temporally aligned robot actions and auxiliary state predictions read from denoised DiT features without pixel decoding. [E08]

steps.name: Construct visible motion trajectories
steps.detail: Action flow contains image coordinates and visibility labels for tracked points over time. For forward deployment, Isaac Lab executes candidate commands to obtain link transforms; sampled robot-surface points are projected through the calibrated camera. Visibility checks depth, image bounds and agreement with a rendered depth buffer. Video-only training data instead use dense tracking and grounded embodiment/object masks.

steps.name: Select the conditioning tracks
steps.detail: Training samples None, Embodiment, Object or All modes with canonical probabilities 0.05, 0.40, 0.40 and 0.15. The mode selects tracks rather than adding a learned mode token. Embodiment/Object use 1–128 tracks; All uses 256–1024. Missing pools trigger probability renormalization, with source-specific overrides.

steps.name: Transport appearance through latent space
steps.detail: Tracks are pooled into latent-frame windows using mean visible positions. Initial-frame features are bilinearly sampled and propagated to future destinations with Gaussian weights. Each destination retains the two largest raw weights; their unnormalized feature sum preserves trajectory mass, while their clipped weight sum supplies a presence gate.

steps.name: Inject motion into the video backbone
steps.detail: Cosmos adds a separately projected 17-channel motion input to video tokens. Wan I2V uses its 16-feature/four-mask visual condition, applying motion conditioning to the high-noise expert and restoring pristine conditioning for the unmodified low-noise expert. Wan TI2V concatenates a constant 49-channel motion input with noisy latents.

steps.name: Roll out causal chunks
steps.detail: Autoregressive conversion uses clean-context teacher forcing and block-causal attention. During generation, previously generated chunks replace clean history and enter a KV cache. Motion conditions are computed in full-window coordinates and sliced at absolute offsets, preserving trajectory alignment across chunk boundaries.

steps.name: Read actions from inverse-mode features
steps.detail: Desired object flow conditions compatible robot motion. Separate action and state heads concatenate mean-pooled and single-query attention-pooled spatial tokens, then apply layer normalization and a two-layer GELU MLP of hidden width 1024. State predictions supply auxiliary supervision and are not fed back into either the video model or action decoder.

training.text: The seven-source corpus contains 1,565,634 retained camera-stream windows, totaling 2,201.7 hours, with an emphasis on deformable interactions. Main windows contain 81 frames at 480p and 16 fps; AllTracker uses a 128 × 128 query grid. DROID and EgoDex lack manipulated-object masks. Static and frozen-gripper filters use a 50-pixel motion floor; filtering combinations vary by source.

Mid-training uses the backbone's flow-matching loss. Pretrained backbone weights are frozen except the patch embedding, with rank-64 LoRA trained on attention q/k/v/o and both feed-forward projections. Wan I2V-A14B training takes 40,000 steps over five days on 32 H100 GPUs.

Causal distillation initializes the student and frozen real-score model from the autoregressive checkpoint. A causal fake-score critic receives five updates per generator update. The student generates seven-latent-frame chunks in four denoising steps; both score branches use zero classifier-free guidance during DMD training.

Inverse post-training updates rank-32 self-attention LoRA, the motion input projection and readout heads. Paired real rollouts can include successes and failures. Action/state targets are normalized per dimension; masked Huber losses accompany a masked L1 loss matching predicted and target action first differences.

inference.text: Ordinary forward deployment derives motion from candidate commands before predicting consequences. The RoboLab experiment instead fixes the complete achieved gripper trajectory from a recorded rollout and starts from its true first observation; policies do not react to generated observations.

Inverse deployment reads actions from final denoised token embeddings without decoding pixels. The reported control configuration uses the 50-step autoregressive teacher, so the few-step student's generation throughput cannot be assigned to the demonstrated controller. The supplied control protocol does not specify a feedback or replanning schedule.

equations.explanation: Equation (1) projects a homogeneous point fixed to robot link ℓ(n) into the camera. Configuration q_t comes from recorded states or the simulated controller rollout; K and T_CW provide camera calibration. This grounds the visual condition in robot motion, without explicitly simulating the object's future deformation.

Equations (8)–(10) implement the motion feature and gate. Here h_n is sampled initial appearance, k indexes latent time, and coordinates share a normalized latent grid. Visibility at both endpoints gates contributions. Weights are neither softmax-normalized nor divided by their sum.

equations.expression: L(θ) = E[||v_θ(Z_t, t, c, C_motion) − v*_t||²]
equations.explanation: Equation (5) trains the video denoiser to match the backbone's target velocity under text/image context c and motion condition C_motion. Here t denotes diffusion time and Z_t the noised target-video latent; this objective does not directly supervise executable actions.

Equation (7) adds supervised action/state readouts to visual flow matching. L_vel matches first differences of normalized action targets over consecutive valid slots; it is not simply a penalty driving action changes toward zero.

results.setting: The same 100 held-out clips per dataset across XVLA-Soft-Fold, Deform360, DROID, MolmoAct2 and ABC-130k. Object EPE averages four strata because DROID object masks are unreliable.
results.metric: Gripper EPE and object EPE in pixels; FVD; lower is better
results.value: Reported Wan2.2 A14B 4-step averages: gripper EPE 3.29 ± 0.10; object EPE 5.27 ± 0.35; FVD 155.9.
results.interpretation: These establish better generated-motion fidelity under the reported protocol, not robot execution success. Backbone, model configuration and conditioning all differ in this strongest comparison; the supplied text does not define the displayed ± statistic.

results.setting: Cosmos 2.5 backbone, with native relative 6D actions versus action flow under the shared dataset mixture and validation protocol.
results.metric: Average gripper/object EPE; FVD; VLM score
results.value: Reported action-flow Cosmos: gripper EPE 13.80 ± 0.85; object EPE 6.27 ± 0.67; FVD 277.4; VLM 3.83 ± 0.05.
results.interpretation: This is the principal mechanism-relevant comparison. Motion and distribution metrics improve, while the displayed VLM average decreases slightly. The VLM rates plausibility and consistency, so it need not track command-following accuracy.

results.setting: Six IWS tasks excluded from mid-training: Bimanual box, Bimanual rope, Bimanual sweep, Push-T, Single chain-in-box and Single grasp. Adaptation uses shared seeded, nested subsets.
results.value: The prose reports that MT outperforms PT on all three metrics for every task at 0% adaptation. Between 20% and 100% data, MT values change by at most 3.4%, 6.7% and 6.8%, respectively.
results.comparison: MT initializes from multi-embodiment mid-training; PT initializes directly from pretrained Wan2.2.
results.interpretation: This supports useful transfer from the additional training stage. Exact curve values were not recoverable. FVD uses 40 clips per point, and the authors caution that its variance prevents interpreting the apparent plateau as strict convergence.

results.setting: One 80-GB H100, bfloat16, batch one, 81 frames at 480 × 832; median of five clips after three warm-ups. Guidance is disabled and VAE decoding excluded.
results.value: Reported few-step student: 1.31 s/clip, 61.98 FPS, 16.0× speedup.
results.comparison: Bidirectional teacher: 20.92 s/clip, 3.87 FPS. Autoregressive teacher: 12.48 s/clip, 6.49 FPS, 1.68× speedup.
results.interpretation: These are generation-only measurements on a short three-chunk horizon; the attention cap is inactive and the bidirectional baseline uses a quantized attention kernel. They do not measure end-to-end control latency. Table 2's LightX2V A14B configuration and this causal student should not be conflated.

results.setting: RoboLab: five policies, six tasks and ten recorded rollouts per policy–task pair, totaling 300 episodes. Generated outcomes are judged by a human blinded to policy identity.
results.metric: Pearson correlation; Spearman correlation; success-rate MAE
results.value: Reported r = 0.96, ρ = 0.93 and MAE = 5.7 percentage points; task-averaged ranking matches all five policies.
results.comparison: Generated-video success judgments versus reference environment success.
results.interpretation: The result measures outcome preservation when replaying achieved trajectories. It does not establish closed-loop policy evaluation. Section 4.5 specifies policy–task comparisons, whereas the introduction describes correlation across five policy aggregates; the aggregation level is not consistently stated.

results.setting: One flexible-pipe-bending task using object flow transferred from a held-out human demonstration; no embodiment flow is supplied.
results.value: The authors report an illustrative successful execution; no trial count, success rate or uncertainty is provided.
results.comparison: No quantitative control baseline is reported.
results.interpretation: This establishes a reported proof of concept for converting latent motion into physical actions. The figure was not visually inspected, and this evidence cannot support broad execution-generalization claims.

limitations.text: The authors report centimeter-scale grasp imprecision and ambiguous grasp/contact states, hypothesizing limited depth awareness as a contributor. Wrist-camera support is only qualitative, and closed-loop policy evaluation remains future work.

Video-only training reduces metadata requirements, but forward command grounding still requires robot geometry and camera calibration. Visibility rendering excludes unknown or unmodeled object occlusions, and the supplied experiments do not quantify sensitivity to calibration error.

ATI and Wan-Move use released checkpoints without Hydra-0's multi-embodiment mid-training. Their comparison therefore combines differences in adaptation and conditioning, rather than isolating architecture or interface alone. No isolated ablation of the four-mode mixture, Gaussian gate or state head is reported.

Inverse-control evidence leaves unresolved how reliably human object flow transfers across camera geometry, initial configurations and contact requirements. A desired image-plane trajectory may not uniquely specify a feasible action sequence.

reproduction.text: Rebuilding the data pipeline requires the seven source datasets, retained window/split identities, captions, tracking and masks. The paper specifies resampling, grid size and motion floors, but not a complete source-specific override/filter configuration or the episode/scene separation underlying every held-out split.

Forward grounding requires matching controller settings, robot geometry and camera calibration. The appendix specifies a 1.2-cm depth-buffer tolerance in a 3 × 3 neighborhood, Gaussian locality 220 and top-two unnormalized aggregation. Learning-rate schedules and full stage-specific optimization settings are not supplied.

Reproducing the control demonstration additionally requires paired action-labeled robot rollouts, target normalization, temporal action-slot alignment, the human-flow transfer procedure and execution scheduling. The supplied text does not give the control-training set size, full action parameterization or repeated-trial protocol.

A focused first test would repeat the same-backbone Cosmos conditioning comparison with identical clips and training budgets, then perturb projected flow to measure calibration sensitivity. A separate repeated pipe-bending study should compare correct, shuffled and absent object-flow conditions using executed success and contact accuracy.

reasoning.text: The WAM and inverse-dynamics interpretation is supported functionally: desired object motion conditions latent robot motion, followed by an embodiment-specific supervised action readout. The Dual-system boundary is less clear. Architecture evidence places action/state heads directly on the shared denoised DiT tokens and does not specify a separate model consuming decoded future frames. This demonstrates integration beyond joint training alone, but the supplied taxonomy does not define whether such heads count as another system. Conversely, Equation (7) does not establish joint diffusion of future-video and action variables. The recorded Q4 classification is therefore preserved but remains unresolved by this audit.

discussionQuestions: How much replay agreement survives when policies react to generated observations and achieved robot trajectories are no longer available in advance? [E15]
Does Object-mode mid-training improve executed control beyond what the pretrained video representation and supervised action head provide? [E04, E08]
Would depth or contact inputs reduce grasp errors while preserving transfer across embodiments and cameras? [E03, E17]
Can the few-step causal student retain the teacher's inverse-action accuracy, and what is its measured end-to-end control latency? [E08, E14]

evidence.location: PDF p. 1, title page, author block and arXiv version stamp
evidence.detail: The title and eleven authors match the supplied catalog identity. The source identifies arXiv:2608.18077v1, dated 18 August 2026, and lists a project-page link.

evidence.location: PDF p. 2, Section 1, motivation, overview and Contributions items 1–4
evidence.detail: The authors motivate image-plane motion by embodiment-dependent command-to-appearance mappings and propose shared forward/inverse use. The introduction describes r = 0.96 across five policy aggregates, creating an aggregation ambiguity with Section 4.5.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 3–4, Section 2.1, Equation (1); PDF p. 21, Section 8.2
evidence.detail: Robot-surface points are propagated through link transforms and calibrated projection. Deployment transforms come from Isaac Lab controller-and-physics rollouts. Visibility requires positive depth, image bounds and depth-buffer agreement within 1.2 cm over a 3 × 3 neighborhood. Unknown object occlusions are not explicitly removed; large projection errors can degrade correspondence.

evidence.location: PDF p. 4, Section 2.1, Video-only construction and Training-time flow sampling; PDF p. 7, Training; PDF pp. 21–22, Section 8.3
evidence.detail: Tracking and grounded masks supply video-derived conditions. Four modes select trajectories without a learned mode token. Canonical probabilities are 0.05/0.40/0.40/0.15 for None/Embodiment/Object/All; track counts are 1–128 or 256–1024. Unavailable pools cause renormalization, with dataset/camera overrides.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 4–5, Section 2.2, Equations (2)–(4); PDF p. 22, Section 8.4, Equations (8)–(10)
evidence.detail: The model predicts future video through an encoder, conditioned latent dynamics and decoder. Pooled tracks transport bilinearly sampled initial features using Gaussian locality 220. Only the top two raw weights contribute; their unnormalized weighted sum forms motion features and their clipped sum forms the gate.

evidence.location: PDF p. 5, Section 2.2, Equation (5) and freezing policy; PDF p. 7, Section 4.1; PDF p. 9, Training continuation; PDF pp. 22–23, Sections 8.5–8.6
evidence.detail: Training uses flow matching, trainable patch embedding and rank-64 attention/feed-forward LoRA. Cosmos uses a 17-channel side input; Wan I2V uses 16 feature and four mask channels with conditioning confined to the adapted high-noise expert; TI2V uses 49 side-input channels. A14B training uses 40,000 steps, five days and 32 H100 GPUs.

evidence.location: PDF p. 5, Section 2.3, Equation (6); PDF p. 23, Sections 8.7–8.8
evidence.detail: Causal conversion uses clean-context teacher forcing, block-causal attention and cached generated history. Motion tensors retain absolute offsets. DMD uses seven-latent chunks, four student denoising steps, causal real/fake score models, five critic updates per generator update and zero guidance in both score branches.

evidence.location: PDF p. 6, Section 2.4, Inverse mode and Equation (7)
evidence.detail: Desired object flow conditions robot motion. Action/state heads pool clean DiT tokens and use normalization plus two-layer width-1024 GELU MLPs. Post-training updates rank-32 self-attention LoRA, motion projection and heads. Normalized masked Huber action/state losses and action-difference L1 loss use weights 0.1 and 0.1. State output is auxiliary; deployment reads denoised tokens without pixels.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 6–7, Section 3 and Table 1, Total row
evidence.detail: Seven datasets yield 1,565,634 retained windows and 2,201.7 hours counted on annotated camera streams. Main windows use 81 frames at 480p/16 fps and a 128 × 128 AllTracker grid. DROID/EgoDex object masks are unavailable. Static and frozen-gripper filters use a 50-pixel floor; a separate DROID wrist stream uses 17-frame windows.

evidence.location: PDF p. 9, Table 2 caption and Section 4.2; PDF p. 10, Section 4.2 protocol and Results
evidence.detail: Methods share 100 validation clips per dataset across five held-out sets. DROID object EPE is omitted. Native-action Cosmos is fine-tuned; ATI and Wan-Move use released checkpoints without multi-embodiment mid-training. The A14B four-step evaluation includes a LightX2V checkpoint. The prose identifies the Cosmos representation comparison as controlled.

evidence.location: PDF p. 9, Table 2, Average block, Cosmos 2.5 and Ours (Wan2.2 A14B 4-step) rows
evidence.detail: Native-action Cosmos reports object EPE 13.23 ± 0.97, gripper EPE 34.28 ± 1.02 and FVD 405.8. A14B four-step reports object EPE 5.27 ± 0.35, gripper EPE 3.29 ± 0.10 and FVD 155.9. Averages are unweighted across available dataset strata.

evidence.location: PDF p. 9, Table 2, Average block, Cosmos 2.5 and Ours (Cosmos 2.5 2B) rows; PDF p. 10, Section 4.2 Results
evidence.detail: Action-flow Cosmos reports object EPE 6.27 ± 0.67, gripper EPE 13.80 ± 0.85, FVD 277.4 and VLM 3.83 ± 0.05. Native-action Cosmos reports 13.23 ± 0.97, 34.28 ± 1.02, 405.8 and 3.88 ± 0.05. The authors distinguish mixed VLM results from improved motion accuracy.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 10–11, Section 4.3, task/subset protocol and Results prose
evidence.detail: IWS is excluded from mid-training; six tasks use common nested adaptation subsets. The prose reports lower zero-shot LPIPS/EPE/FVD for MT than PT on all tasks. From 20% to 100% data, maximum per-task changes are 3.4%/6.7%/6.8%. FVD uses 40 clips per point and is described as high variance.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 11–12, Section 4.4, Protocol and Results; PDF p. 12, Table 3
evidence.detail: On one 80-GB H100, generation-only timing for 81 frames at 480 × 832 gives 20.92/12.48/1.31 seconds and 3.87/6.49/61.98 FPS for bidirectional teacher, autoregressive teacher and student. Guidance and VAE decoding are excluded; the three-chunk horizon does not exercise the attention cap. The control model uses the 50-step autoregressive teacher.

evidence.location: PDF p. 6, Section 2.4, Forward mode; PDF p. 12, Section 4.5, Protocol and Results
evidence.detail: Replay fixes complete recorded gripper motion and starts from the true first observation without querying policies on generated frames. RoboLab covers five policies, six tasks and ten rollouts per pair, totaling 300 episodes. Section 4.5 describes policy–task comparisons and reports r = 0.96, ρ = 0.93, MAE 5.7 percentage points and matching task-averaged policy ranking.

evidence.location: PDF p. 13, Section 4.6 and Figure 10 caption
evidence.detail: The qualitative control study uses one flexible-pipe-bending task. Desired object flow comes from a held-out human demonstration; embodiment flow is excluded. A trained action head converts latent rollout features to commands. The caption reports successful execution, but the text supplies no repeated-trial success rate or control baseline.

The authors identify centimeter-scale grasp imprecision, hypothesized insufficient depth awareness, and ambiguous grasp/contact states. Depth, tactile and force sensing are proposed directions. Wrist-camera evidence is qualitative, and closed-loop policy evaluation remains future work.

evidence.location: PDF p. 23, Section 8.9, VLM Judge Details
evidence.detail: Gemma 4 31B uses deterministic decoding and 16 uniformly spaced frames from each 81-frame generated clip. It rates physical plausibility, temporal consistency, object permanence and motion realism on a 1–5 scale; ratings are averaged within and across clips.
